Also turbotab/core/estimand.py:1432-1442, 1532-1616.

statement: Under inference, cross-validated fit scores (R2, RMSE, MAE, calibration, optimism) describe the outcome model's fit, not the reported estimate, and reading them before the adjustment set is answered is one more fork in the analysis path, so they are withheld while the plan is open.
regime: inference; plan open
user_sees: Its cross-validated scores (R2, RMSE, MAE and the rest) wait too: under inference they describe the outcome model's fit, not the reported estimate.
claimed_basis: Gelman & Loken 2013; MODELING_SEQUENCE §1 row 11 ('not a comparison') and §0 ruling 13
notes: Also turbotab/core/estimand.py:1504-1529. Merged duplicate: models/survey.py:1203 states the same withholding under inference (MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 13, §1 row 11).

statement: Under prediction no coefficient is read as an effect, so no exposure, estimand, adjustment set, model sequence or diagnostic response is declared and these answers are refused.
regime: prediction
user_sees: Under prediction no coefficient is read as an effect, so an adjustment set does not arise; it is asked under inference.
claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE organizing fact
notes: Also turbotab/core/estimand.py:485-490.

statement: Under the modified disjunctive cause criterion for a total effect, a pre-exposure covariate that is, or may be, a cause of the exposure, of the outcome, or of both is adjusted for in the primary model, a cause of the exposure only included.
regime: inference; total effect; covariate not changed by the exposure
decision: each covariate's derived role and inclusion
user_sees: a cause of what you study: the criterion adjusts for it | a possible cause of what you study and of the outcome: the criterion adjusts for it
claimed_basis: VanderWeele 2019, Eur J Epidemiol 34:211 ('control for each covariate that is a cause of the exposure, or of the outcome, or of both'); MODELING_SEQUENCE §1 step 3
notes: test_wp17_purpose_routes.py::test_3_the_criterion_derives_each_role_from_the_answers checks the mapping against the quoted rule (implementation), not validity. 'Unknown' answers default to confounder. VanderWeele notes pure exposure causes can cost precision and amplify bias from residual confounding.

statement: A covariate that is a cause of the outcome only is adjusted for in the primary model because adjusting for it sharpens the estimate.
regime: inference; total effect; any outcome family
decision: precision covariate's inclusion and its stated reason
user_sees: a cause of the outcome only: adjusting for it sharpens the estimate
claimed_basis: VanderWeele 2019
notes: True for a linear model; under logistic or Cox the conditional estimate moves away from the null and its SE typically grows (Robinson & Jewell 1991), and the estimand changes (see the non-collapsibility entry). Also turbotab/core/estimand.py:899 (GUESS_WORDS).

statement: A covariate that is a cause of neither the exposure nor the outcome is left out of the adjustment set.
regime: inference; total effect
user_sees: a cause of neither what you study nor the outcome: the criterion leaves it out
claimed_basis: VanderWeele 2019

statement: A known instrument (it affects the outcome only through the exposure) is left out of the adjustment set, because adjusting for it amplifies any confounding that remains.
regime: inference; covariate answered an instrument
user_sees: a known instrument: it moves the outcome only through what you study, and adjusting for it amplifies any confounding left
claimed_basis: VanderWeele 2019 ('exclude from this set any variable known to be an instrumental variable')
notes: Bias amplification (Pearl 2010; Myers et al. 2011) is implied but not cited.

statement: An instrument affects the outcome only through the exposure and is a cause of the exposure, so a covariate answered both an instrument and a cause of the outcome, or an instrument but not a cause of the exposure, is inconsistent and refused.
regime: inference; adjustment answers
user_sees: `z` is answered an instrument but not a cause of what you study; an instrument is one.
claimed_basis: none stated (definition)
notes: IV relevance requires association with the exposure, not necessarily causation (a proxy of a cause qualifies), so the second refusal is stricter than the definition.

statement: A proxy for an unmeasured common cause of the exposure and the outcome is adjusted for.
regime: inference
user_sees: a proxy for an unmeasured cause of both
claimed_basis: VanderWeele 2019 ('include as a covariate any proxy for an unmeasured variable that is a common cause')

statement: For a total effect, a covariate the exposure could have changed (or measured after it) that causes the outcome is a mediator, and adjusting for it removes part of the total effect, so keeping it in the total-effect set is blocked and recorded and 'further adjusted for' it is offered as a labeled secondary (Model 3) that is not a total effect.
regime: inference; total effect; covariate answered after the exposure and a cause of the outcome
decision: whether a mediator may stay in the primary set
user_sees: `hdl` is a mediator by your answers: in a total-effect set it removes part of the effect, or opens a path that is not causal (VanderWeele 2019...: what could explain the link 'ought to be controlled f
claimed_basis: VanderWeele 2019; MODELING_SEQUENCE §4 (mediators in a total-effect set: block and record)
notes: Model 3/secondary notes say 'possible mediators: not a total effect'. Also turbotab/core/estimand.py:716-724, turbotab/core/stages/effects.py:998-1003, turbotab/core/stages/secondary.py:1-9.

statement: For a total effect, a covariate the exposure could have changed but that does not cause the outcome is a consequence of the exposure (a possible collider) and is left out, because adjusting for it can open a path that is not causal; keeping it is blocked and recorded.
regime: inference; total effect; covariate answered after the exposure, not a cause of the outcome
user_sees: changed by what you study without causing the outcome: adjusting for it can open a path that is not causal
claimed_basis: VanderWeele 2019
notes: Adjusting for a pure descendant of the exposure opens a non-causal path only if the outcome (or a cause of the outcome) also affects it; otherwise it costs precision but adds no bias. The docstring says 'a collider when the outcome changes it too', but the answers never ask that. Also turbotab/core/estimand.py:2115-2143.

statement: A covariate whose timing relative to the exposure is unknown (such as a cross-sectional BMI) cannot be classed as a confounder or a mediator from the data, so for a total effect the primary model excludes it and a declared secondary model further adjusted for it is reported beside it (the with-and-without pair).
regime: inference; total effect; covariate answered 'could the exposure have changed it: unknown'
decision: covariate inclusion and the secondary model
user_sees: possible mediator, or measured after what you study: the estimate is declared without it and, beside, with it
claimed_basis: VanderWeele 2019 ('We cannot adequately distinguish in this setting between confounding and mediation'); MODELING_SEQUENCE §1 step 3
notes: The packs guess body size, clinical measurements and medications measured with the exposure as unknown timing (covariate_guesses.py, other slice). Putting the 'without' model as primary is the app's choice. Also turbotab/core/estimand.py:900-901, turbotab/core/stages/secondary.py:1-15.

statement: Other dietary components default to (possible) confounders of a dietary exposure through the diet's shared common causes, never to 'not relevant'.
regime: inference; dietary lens; other nutrients among the covariates
user_sees: Other dietary components: they share the diet's common causes with what you study, so they default to ...
claimed_basis: NUTRITION_PACK §08 (Model 4: mutually adjusted nutrients); MODELING_SEQUENCE §1 step 3
notes: Primary registry is turbotab/core/covariate_guesses.py:104-109 (other slice; possible duplicate). A nutrient on the causal path, or part of the same total as the exposure, would not be a confounder.

statement: A measurement of the outcome's own kind taken at the same visit as the exposure is a consequence of the exposure (a descending proxy for an intermediate) and is left out of the adjustment set; at baseline beside an outcome measured over follow-up it is the with-and-without pair.
regime: inference; covariate of the outcome's own kind
user_sees: another measure of the outcome's own kind, which the study factor could have changed: left out
claimed_basis: Schisterman ('a descending proxy for an intermediate variable'); NUTRITION_PACK §08
notes: Registry in covariate_guesses.py:135-141 (other slice). Also turbotab/core/estimand.py:58-62, 903-904.

statement: For an energy-bearing exposure with total energy in the model, a substitution (more of it in place of other calories, total energy fixed) and an addition (its calories added, every other source fixed) are different estimands, so the contrast must be declared before estimates.
regime: inference; energy-bearing exposure; total energy among the predictors
user_sees: `sugar` carries energy and total energy is in the model: say whether its effect is a substitution (...) or an addition (...). The two are different comparisons (Tomova et al. 2022).
claimed_basis: Tomova et al. 2022
notes: Overlaps the energy slice.

statement: Under inference a substitution contrast is estimated by the standard, residual (energy kept or dropped), all-components, density and multivariate-density energy models, and an addition contrast only by the partition or all-components model, so an energy model that does not estimate the declared contrast is refused, with all-components ranked first.
regime: inference; energy-bearing exposure; declared contrast
user_sees: The comparison you want is a substitution of `sugar`'s calories, and the partition model estimates no substitution (Tomova et al. 2022).
claimed_basis: Tomova et al. 2022; BLUEPRINT §12 rulings 1-2
notes: Listing the energy-dropped residual and the density models as substitution estimators is questionable: BLUEPRINT §12 ruling 1 says each form has its own estimand (McCullough & Byrd 2023), and the density model's coefficient is per unit of density. Overlaps the energy slice.

statement: When the primary analysis excludes rows (for example by a screen for implausible energy reports), the same model fit on the total sample without exclusions should also be reported beside it, so the impact of the screen can be seen.
regime: any purpose; primary exclusion rules present and no named analysis keeps every row
user_sees: The every-row analysis was added because the primary excludes rows. Banna et al. 2017: 'analyses in the total sample without exclusion of participants should also be conducted and reported'.
claimed_basis: Banna et al. 2017, Front Nutr 4:45
notes: Each analysis refits the whole pipeline (energy model, imputation) on its own rows 'so the analyses differ only by their rows' (turbotab/core/stages/sensitivity.py:20-21). Also turbotab/core/stages/sensitivity.py:464-465. Merged duplicate: methods/misreporting.py:24-26 cites Banna et al. 2017 for the same rule ('analyses in the total sample without exclusion of participants should also be conducted and reported').

statement: An exclusion rule that reads the outcome (its column, ranges set by it, or any input of a Goldberg screen that is the outcome) selects on the value being explained and biases the estimates, so it is refused in each sensitivity analysis as in the primary.
regime: any purpose; exclusion rules
user_sees: A rule reads the outcome `bmi`. Keeping rows by their outcome selects on the value being explained, which biases the estimates, and no one whose outcome is still unknown could be screened by it.
claimed_basis: audit RO-01; BLUEPRINT §12 (RO-01 guard)
notes: OUTCOME_RULE text lives in turbotab/core/decisions.py:3804 (other slice; possible duplicate). Merged duplicate: methods/misreporting.py:27-29 cites Banna et al. 2017 ('body weight is included in both the calculation of implausible rEI and the outcome variable … which could artificially elevate the association'); the |r| >= 0.5 warning for a correlated outcome is S6-070.

statement: When the outcome correlates at |r| >= 0.5 with the body weight a Goldberg screen reads to estimate BMR, excluding rows by that screen selects partly on the outcome and can artificially elevate the association.
regime: a Goldberg energy-misreporting screen in any analysis; outcome not the weight itself
user_sees: `bmi` correlates 0.62 with `weight`, which the Goldberg screen reads to estimate BMR: excluding by it selects partly on the outcome (Banna et al. 2017).
claimed_basis: Banna et al. 2017 (weight 'is included in both the calculation of implausible rEI and the outcome variable ... which could artificially elevate the association'); WEIGHT_CORRELATION = 0.5 app convention
notes: Also turbotab/core/stages/sensitivity.py:24-27, 44.

statement: Under inference every analysis (primary, declared sequence, secondary and sensitivity analyses) is estimated on all eligible rows, held-out rows included, because a holdout is a prediction concept and inference needs every row with honest intervals.
regime: inference
decision: which rows the inference analyses use
user_sees: the same model was refit on all eligible rows for each sensitivity analysis
claimed_basis: BLUEPRINT §12 ruling 3 ('The seal is purpose-scoped. Inference estimates from all eligible rows, with honest intervals; a holdout is a prediction concept')
notes: Also turbotab/core/stages/sensitivity.py:361, turbotab/core/stages/secondary.py:11, 100, turbotab/core/stages/effects.py:39-40. Likely duplicated in the split/seal slice. Doc: BLUEPRINT §12 ruling 3 ('The seal is purpose-scoped. Inference estimates from all eligible rows, with honest intervals; a holdout is a prediction concept'); also seal.py:613 (INFERENCE_SPLIT_REASON, citing Shmueli 2010) and stages/modeling.py:12-16 (twenty random 80% seals moved the NHANES sugar coefficient from -0.097 to -0.021).

statement: Under a prediction purpose no fitted coefficient can be read as a causal effect, so the causal lane (DML, TMLE, post-double-selection lasso) and the time-varying g-methods lane are refused and offered only under inference.
regime: purpose = prediction; any outcome
user_sees: Under prediction no coefficient is read as an effect, so no causal estimate is offered; the causal lane is asked under inference.
claimed_basis: BLUEPRINT §11.3 ('a causal question gets a shorter leash than exploratory prediction'); MODELING_SEQUENCE §2 relation prediction_refuses
notes: Also causal.py:140 (relation), 321-323 (plan_reason), 237 (contract sound text); time_varying.py:336-338 and 144-145/155-156/165-166 (same reason for the g-methods). acceptance test_6 only checks the refusal code.

statement: The causal lane's estimators, fit over the adjustment set the disjunctive-cause answers keep (mediators left out), estimate the exposure's total effect; a declared direct effect needs mediation methods and is refused there.
regime: inference; estimand effect = direct
user_sees: A direct effect needs mediation methods, which the causal lane does not fit; it estimates the total effect.
claimed_basis: none stated (plan_reason)
notes: The methods sentence heads 'The {effect} effect of x on y was also estimated' (causal.py:719), which can then only be total.

statement: When the declared exposure changes over time within units, a point-exposure estimate by DML, TMLE or post-double selection is biased, as standard regression is, by confounders that earlier exposure changed, so the causal lane is refused and the time-varying lane's g-methods are required.
regime: inference; long data (a unit's time points as rows); exposure varies within at least one unit
user_sees: `x` changes over time within units, so its effect is estimated by the time-varying lane's g-methods; the causal lane estimates the effect of a study factor measured once.
claimed_basis: Robins, Hernán & Brumback 2000 (cited in the time-varying lane); MODELING_SEQUENCE §2 relation time_varying_exposure (Wave 2a)
notes: The refusal fires whenever exposure_varies is true (time_varying.py:361-369), whether or not any covariate is answered as a confounder affected by prior exposure; the time-varying lane itself recommends standard regression when none is (stages/time_varying.py:291-299), so the stated bias is unconditional where the method's own condition is not. Also causal.py:205-211, 360-362, 379-382.

statement: Data-adaptive adjustment (cross-fitted DML/TMLE nuisance learners, the post-double-selection lasso) gives valid post-selection inference for the exposure effect when the learners and lassos choose only among the candidate covariates the subject-knowledge adjustment answers keep, never among those they leave out; any other data-driven selection is refused under inference.
regime: inference; adjustment set answered by the disjunctive cause criterion
decision: the candidate set for set_causal; data-driven selection under set_adjustment
user_sees: Selection by the data is refused under inference except rung (d): the lasso and the learners choose only among the covariates the answers adjust for, never among those they leave out.
claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 1 rung (d); §1 row 3
notes: acceptance test_6 asserts the mediator ldl is not among the candidates (code behavior). The candidate matrix also carries total energy and grouping fixed effects (stages/causal.py:332-336). Doc: MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 1(d) (data-adaptive adjustment with valid post-selection inference is allowed; ranks high when candidates are many relative to n, S7-005).

statement: The candidate adjustment terms are 'many relative to n' when they exceed one per 10 of the limiting sample size (all rows for a numeric outcome; the rarer outcome level's count for a yes/no outcome), and then, for a numeric outcome, the post-double-selection lasso should rank first among all the causal estimators (above DML and TMLE, whatever the exposure type).
regime: inference; numeric outcome; not the surveyed-population answer
decision: ranking of set_causal options and the Router's stated reason
user_sees: with 120 candidate terms for a limiting sample size of 300 (more than one per 10), post-double-selection lasso ranks first and is one step away.
claimed_basis: Harrell, Regression Modeling Strategies (2015) §4.4 (about one parameter per 10 of n); MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 1 rung (d) ('ranks high when the candidates are many relative to n')
notes: Harrell's 10:1 is an overfitting rule for unpenalized models, repurposed as the switch to PDS; DML with lasso nuisances also handles many candidates, so 'ranks first' is a ranking choice, not a validity result. options() gives PDS rank 0 for a yes/no exposure too (causal.py:435-441), above TMLE. Candidates are model-matrix columns (one-hot levels count). test_3 only checks the ranking code. Also causal.py:102, 344-357; stages/causal.py:349-354, 519-529.

statement: With many candidate covariates relative to n (e.g. 120 or 300 candidates for 100 rows), selecting controls by both the outcome lasso and the exposure lasso and refitting least squares on the union (post-double selection) keeps the exposure coefficient's 95% interval approximately valid, unlike single-selection post-model inference.
regime: inference; numeric outcome; candidates many relative to n; independent unweighted rows
decision: 'sound' label and first rank for pds_lasso
user_sees: many candidates for n: selecting by both lassos keeps the intervals valid
claimed_basis: Belloni, Chernozhukov & Hansen 2014 (abstract quoted at models/causal.py:40-43); simulation in test_3b
notes: Known-truth simulation: 1,000 data sets, n = 100, p = 120 and 300, Toeplitz, sparse (4 relevant), homoskedastic; it requires coverage >= 90% for nominal 95% (hdm about 93%), so sub-nominal coverage passes. Also contract sound text causal.py:293-294.

statement: With few candidate covariates relative to n, post-double selection is still valid but has little to select, so it ranks below DML in the partially linear model (and, for a yes/no exposure, below TMLE and the interactive model).
regime: inference; numeric outcome; candidates at most one per 10 of the limiting n
user_sees: with few candidates for n there is little to select; valid all the same
claimed_basis: BCH 2014 (source); none stated for the ordering
notes: Ranked 5, 'conditional'.

statement: The post-double-selection lasso's plug-in penalty is derived for independent, unweighted rows, so its selection cannot carry survey weights; under the surveyed-population answer it is blocked and recorded, with the survey-weighted DML partially linear model or an unweighted, sample-only estimate as the exits.
regime: inference; survey design with the population estimand
user_sees: The estimate is for the surveyed population, and the post-double-selection lasso's plug-in penalty is derived for independent, unweighted rows: its selection cannot carry the survey weights.
claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 6 (no design-based estimator: block and record); BCH 2014
notes: Also causal.py:37-41, 169-173, 436-438 (ranked 6, 'unsound'); stages/causal.py:675-681. The sample-only sentence says the estimate 'describes these participants only' (causal.py:784-788).

statement: The post-double-selection lasso is a linear model of the outcome, so it is not used for a yes/no outcome; TMLE or the interactive DML model estimate the risk difference there.
regime: inference; yes/no outcome
user_sees: The post-double-selection lasso is a linear model of the outcome; for a yes/no outcome TMLE or the interactive DML model estimate the risk difference.
claimed_basis: none stated
notes: Also contract needs 'a numeric outcome' (causal.py:284); options() adds PDS only for task = regression (435). A linear-probability PDS would also estimate a risk difference, and DML-PLR on a yes/no outcome is allowed in linear-probability form, so this is a scope choice stated as a modeling reason.

statement: After double selection, least squares of the outcome on the exposure and the union of selected controls with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (not hdm's HC1-type) gives valid normal-reference 95% intervals for the exposure's coefficient.
regime: inference; numeric outcome; independent rows
user_sees: ... and the outcome was regressed on `x` and the union, with HC3 standard errors
claimed_basis: 'the app's heteroskedasticity-robust standard for a linear model; Long & Ervin 2000' (models/causal.py:39-41); MacKinnon & White 1985
notes: test_3b's coverage uses the HC3 SE but its design is homoskedastic; test_3's heteroskedastic case only checks HC3 against a hand formula. test_3c says the SEs differ from hdm's by design.

statement: The heteroskedastic plug-in lasso with penalty 2c√n Φ⁻¹(1 − γ/(2p)), c = 1.1, γ = 0.1/ln n, loadings started from the residuals on the 5 columns most correlated with the response, a first fit at λ/2 and loadings iterated from post-lasso residuals (hdm 0.3.2 rlasso defaults) is the selection step of BCH's post-double-selection estimator; starting the loadings from y − ȳ instead over-penalizes the columns that carry the signal.
regime: inference; numeric outcome
user_sees: plug-in lassos over the p declared model terms of the covariates selected ... for the outcome and ... for the exposure
claimed_basis: Belloni, Chen, Chernozhukov & Hansen 2012 Algorithm A.1; hdm 0.3.2 source; test_3b docstring ('started from y − ȳ at the full penalty covered 49% to 75% here')
notes: test_3c (skips without R hdm) and test_3 (a hand transcription of hdm) test that the code computes hdm's estimator; the 'over-penalizes' claim rests on the in-repo simulation note. Also models/causal.py:33-38, 965-1001.

statement: For a numeric exposure, double/debiased ML in the partially linear model Y = θD + g(X) + ε, with the partialling-out orthogonal score, K-fold cross-fitted nuisance learners (dml2) and variance mean(ψ²)/J²/n, gives a root-n-consistent θ with valid normal-reference 95% intervals even with flexible learners (cross-validated lasso, random forest, untuned boosted trees).
regime: inference; numeric exposure; numeric or yes/no outcome
decision: first-ranked option and the PLR estimate
user_sees: orthogonal score with cross-fitting: valid intervals with flexible learners
claimed_basis: Chernozhukov et al. 2018, Econom J 21:C1; as R DoubleML 1.0.2 computes it
notes: test_1a (lm learners, 1e-6) and test_1b (cv_glmnet, Monte Carlo tolerance) test that the code computes DoubleML's estimator, plus one data set within 3 SE of the truth; no coverage check, and none with the forest or boosted-tree learners, whose rates the validity needs. Also causal.py:256-257, models/causal.py:9-21, 630-671.

statement: For a yes/no exposure with heterogeneous effects, the partially linear model's θ is an average of conditional effects weighted by the exposure's residual variance Var(D|X), not the average effect over everyone, so it ranks below TMLE and the interactive model, and its methods sentence says so.
regime: inference; yes/no exposure
user_sees: for a yes/no study factor it estimates a variance-weighted average, not the average effect
claimed_basis: none stated beyond Chernozhukov et al. 2018
notes: Also causal.py:256-257 and 720-727 ('averaged with weights by the exposure's residual variance rather than over everyone').

statement: For a yes/no exposure, double/debiased ML in the interactive model with the doubly robust (AIPW) scores for the ATE and the ATT (p the test fold's exposed share), cross-fitted propensity and outcome models and dml2, gives valid normal-reference intervals with flexible learners.
regime: inference; yes/no exposure; numeric or yes/no outcome
decision: rank 2 option and the IRM estimate
user_sees: doubly robust score with cross-fitting: valid intervals with flexible learners
claimed_basis: Chernozhukov et al. 2018; as R DoubleML 1.0.2 computes it
notes: Implementation check against DoubleML (ATE and ATTE) only; coverage not tested. Also causal.py:267-269, models/causal.py:674-745.

statement: For a yes/no exposure, targeted maximum likelihood should rank above DML's interactive model because it is doubly robust, efficient, and, as a substitution estimator, keeps each estimate inside the outcome's range.
regime: inference; yes/no exposure; numeric or yes/no outcome
decision: first-ranked option for a yes/no exposure
user_sees: doubly robust, efficient, and keeps each estimate inside the outcome's range
claimed_basis: Schuler & Rose 2017 (customary); van der Laan & Rubin 2006
notes: AIPW (DML-IRM) is also doubly robust and efficient, so the ordering rests on boundedness. Contract sound text causal.py:281.

statement: Truncating the propensity at b = 5/(√n ln n) (tmle's default; Gruber et al. 2022) is an appropriate bound for both TMLE (each level, below) and DML's interactive model ([b, 1 − b]), and the same b defines the band whose violation the positivity check counts.
regime: inference; yes/no exposure
decision: the propensity bound in TMLE and DML-IRM
user_sees: with the propensity truncated below at 0.0177 for each level (Gruber et al. 2022, Am J Epidemiol 191:1640)
claimed_basis: Gruber, Phillips, Lee & van der Laan 2022; tmle 2.1.1 default
notes: DoubleML's own default trimming threshold is 0.01; the app passes tmle's n-dependent b to dml_irm (stages/causal.py:697, 755-757). test_1a and test_2 use the same bound on both sides, so they check implementation only. TMLE truncates g1 and g0 below only (models/causal.py:838-839).

statement: With a flexible learner, cross-fitting TMLE's initial outcome model Q and propensity g on the sample splits and fitting one pooled logistic fluctuation over all rows (the pooled cross-validated TMLE), with influence-curve variance var(IC)/n and DoubleML's median aggregation over repeated splits, gives valid intervals for the average effect.
regime: inference; yes/no exposure; learner lasso, random forest or boosted trees (the defaults are never linear)
user_sees: random forests ... modeled the outcome and the propensity given the covariates, each fit on the other 4 of 5 folds, ... and the interval is read off the influence curve
claimed_basis: Zheng & van der Laan 2011 (models/causal.py:30-31)
notes: No test compares the cross-fitted TMLE with an independent reference or checks its coverage; test_causal_learners only checks factory == name. This is the default TMLE path (S7-035).

statement: Over S repeated sample splits, the median estimate with se = sqrt(median(n·se_s² + (θ_s − θ̃)²)/n) gives a split-robust estimate and a standard error that accounts for split-to-split variation; the app applies it to DML, to cross-fitted TMLE and to the interactive model's log risk ratio.
regime: inference; repetitions >= 1
user_sees: the estimate is the median over 3 random sample splits
claimed_basis: DoubleML's agg_cross_fit (Chernozhukov et al. 2018)
notes: test_1a matches DoubleML for DML (implementation). Using the same rule for TMLE and for log RR (models/causal.py:739, 927) is the app's extension; PLR's robustness value is also a median over splits (causal.py:576-579).

statement: A regression of the outcome on the exposure adjusted for a set chosen from subject knowledge is nutritional epidemiology's analysis and is valid when the outcome model's functional form is right, so it is the declared primary analysis and the causal ML estimators are stated one step away rather than asked by default.
regime: inference; one declared exposure; adjustment answered
decision: Router default for the causal question (skipped, stated) and option 'none'
user_sees: valid when the outcome model's form is right; the lane checks that
claimed_basis: Walter & Tiemeier 2009 (customary); causal_gate docstring
notes: 'the lane checks that' is vague: nothing compares the primary model's form with the lane's estimate or flags a disagreement. 'none' is ranked last (9) yet is the Router's default (STATED, causal.py:340-341, 365-396).

statement: A causal effect estimate rests on four identification assumptions (no unmeasured confounding given the adjustment set, positivity, consistency as one well-defined intervention, and time ordering), of which no unmeasured confounding cannot be confirmed by any data, so each is declared beside its diagnostic before any estimate is computed.
regime: inference; causal lane
user_sees: The causal estimate rests on assumptions the data cannot check, so each is declared before any estimate is shown.
claimed_basis: Hernán & Robins 2020, What If §3.1–3.5
notes: The refusal says the data 'cannot check' them, yet positivity has a data diagnostic and the card marks it 'checked' or 'violated'. 'Time ordering' is not one of What If ch. 3's three conditions (exchangeability, positivity, consistency); check the citation. Also causal.py:26-29, 92-99, 456-511; stages/causal.py:633-638.

statement: For a yes/no exposure's average effect, when 1% or more of the rows (the survey-weighted share under a design) have an estimated propensity outside [b, 1 − b], b = 5/(√n ln n), positivity is practically violated and the estimate leans on extrapolation for a visible part of the sample, so it is refused until the rows are trimmed or every row is kept on the record.
regime: inference; yes/no exposure; any causal method
decision: set_causal (positivity) and the stage's withheld estimate
user_sees: 1,234 of 1,500 rows (x%, at or above the lane's line of 1%) have a propensity outside [b, 1 − b], the bound the estimator caps at: for them one level ... is all but impossible given the covariates
claimed_basis: 'A convention of this app'; Petersen et al. 2012 set no universal threshold; Hernán & Robins 2020 §3.3
notes: test_4a only checks violated == share >= 1% (the code's rule). The decision gate reads the card's cross-fitted main-terms logistic propensity (stages/causal.py:498-511) even for a forest estimator; the stage re-reads with the estimator's own (689-716), so they can disagree; under PDS a yes/no exposure is checked by an every-row logistic fit (702-705). Also causal.py:30-36, 156-160, 1057-1069; stages/causal.py:551-569.

statement: For the effect among the exposed (ATT), only rows with a propensity above 1 − b threaten positivity (exposed-like rows with no comparable unexposed row); rows with a propensity near 0 are never extrapolated to, so the ATT is not refused for them.
regime: inference; yes/no exposure; DML-IRM with population = exposed
user_sees: For the effect among the exposed, k of n rows ... have a propensity above 1 − b, the bound the estimator caps at: for them not being exposed is all but impossible given the covariates
claimed_basis: none stated beyond Hernán & Robins 2020 §3.3
notes: test_9 checks the gate's behavior and the card's share against an independent logistic fit (implementation). Also models/causal.py:1141; stages/causal.py:507-511, 556-563.

statement: For a numeric exposure, a cross-fitted R² of 0.9 or more of the exposure on the covariates (a variance inflation factor of 10) is a practical positivity violation: the effect rests on little of the exposure's own variation and extrapolates where it does not vary, so the estimate is refused until every row is kept on the record.
regime: inference; numeric exposure; DML-PLR or PDS
user_sees: The covariates explain 93% of `x`'s variance (at least 90%, a variance inflation factor of 10 or more): the effect rests on little of the variation of what you study itself, and the estimate extrapol…
claimed_basis: Kutner, Nachtsheim & Neter 2004 §10.5 (VIF 10, 'the conventional line'); the app's convention
notes: VIF 10 is a collinearity rule of thumb, not a positivity criterion: a global R² does not show whether the exposure varies at every covariate level. The record is the only exit (no trimming for a numeric exposure). Also stages/causal.py:512-518, 584-588, 736-748.

statement: For a yes/no exposure with a practical positivity violation, trimming to the rows whose estimated propensity lies in [0.1, 0.9] (Crump, Hotz, Imbens & Mitnik 2009's rule of thumb) is a sound way forward, giving a well-defined, more precisely estimated average effect in the overlap population.
regime: inference; yes/no exposure; DML-IRM or TMLE; positivity violated
decision: the trimming exit and its level (TRIM_AT)
user_sees: Trim to propensities in [0.1, 0.9] (the overlap population)
claimed_basis: Crump et al. 2009, Biometrika 96:187
notes: Crump et al.'s 0.1 approximates the variance-minimizing overlap set for the ATE under homoskedasticity. The app trims on the estimator's own propensity and re-cross-fits on the kept rows (stages/causal.py:702-735). Trimming is refused for PLR, PDS or a numeric exposure (causal.py:986-992). test_4b checks the trimmed TMLE equals R tmle on the kept rows (implementation). Also causal.py:91; models/causal.py:1185-1189.

statement: Under the surveyed-population answer, entering the survey weights in every nuisance fit and in the estimating equation (Σ wᵢψᵢ(θ) = 0; tmle's obsWeights), dealing whole PSUs to folds, and taking the Taylor-linearized variance of the weighted score over strata and PSUs (with-replacement PSUs, t on PSUs − strata df, out-of-domain rows at score zero) gives design-consistent population estimates and valid intervals for DML and TMLE.
regime: inference; survey design; population estimand
decision: the lane's estimate and variance under a design
user_sees: The survey weight `w` entered every nuisance fit and the estimating equation, the folds kept each PSU's rows together, and the variance is linearized over the design's strata and PSUs.
claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 6; R survey svyglm/svymean; NHANES Analytic Guidelines 2011–2016 §3.2.3.1 (domains)
notes: Partial: test_5 checks the code equals R survey on the same cross-fitted nuisances (implementation) and, on one simulated sample, that weighted TMLE covers the population effect while unweighted does not. The variance treats the nuisances as fixed. Also causal.py:37-41, 164-168, 777-780; models/causal.py:54-59, 106-182, 537-544.

statement: When rows belong together (a site, a household, a unit's repeated rows), keeping each group's rows in one cross-fitting fold (and in each inner lasso CV fold) and taking a cluster-robust variance by group (the design linearization with the cluster as PSU, on t(G − 1)), refused below the unit floor, gives valid intervals for the causal lane.
regime: inference; clusters or repeated units
decision: folds and variance of the lane under clusters
user_sees: The folds kept each `site`'s rows together, and the variance is cluster-robust by `site`.
claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE §2 ('repeated units or clusters imply cluster-aware intervals'); RECIPES F9 (inner folds)
notes: test_5 checks the clustered PLR equals R svyglm(ids = ~psu) (implementation). The variance is the G/(G − 1)-scaled linearization, not the CR2 with Bell–McCaffrey df that MODELING_SEQUENCE §2 asks for repeated units. test_causal_lasso_folds checks units stay whole (behavior). Floor: models.inference.min_clusters (other slice). Also models/causal.py:204-230, 312-320; stages/causal.py:387-393.

statement: Under a fill or multiple-imputation answer, the causal estimates would need pooling over imputations, which the lane does not do, so incomplete rows are blocked until the analyst records running on the complete rows, an analysis valid assuming the complete rows represent the rest; under the complete-case answer the lane runs on the complete rows 'as complete cases do'.
regime: inference; missing values in the outcome, the exposure or an adjusted covariate
user_sees: ... would need every causal estimate pooled over imputations, which the causal lane does not do in v2; it can run on the 1,200 complete rows, assuming they represent the rest.
claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE §2 relation mi_blocks
notes: 'assuming they represent the rest' is an MCAR-type wording; the condition that makes complete cases valid for an adjusted marginal effect is for the referee. Also causal.py:42-45, 178-181, 1112-1126.

statement: DML and TMLE estimate a marginal effect while the odds ratio is non-collapsible, so a declared odds ratio for a yes/no outcome is a different (conditional) estimand; the lane refuses it and its measure for a yes/no outcome is the marginal risk difference.
regime: inference; yes/no outcome; declared measure odds_ratio
user_sees: DML and TMLE estimate a marginal effect, and the declared measure is the odds ratio (non-collapsible): a different comparison. The marginal risk difference is the causal lane's measure for a yes/no o…
claimed_basis: none stated (relation measure_marginal)
notes: The relation (causal.py:188-191) also names a conditional hazard ratio, but time-to-event outcomes are refused outright (333-336). TMLE still reports a marginal odds ratio beside the RD (models/causal.py:952-959).

statement: A numeric exposure declared as a spline or as quintiles enters as several terms while the lane estimates one effect per unit, so the lane refuses it until the exposure's form is declared linear.
regime: inference; numeric exposure; exposure form spline or quintiles
user_sees: `x` is declared as a spline, several terms, and the causal lane estimates one effect per unit of it.
claimed_basis: relation form_single
notes: Implicit claim: the PLR/PDS per-unit θ is meaningful only under a linear exposure form (under a nonlinear dose-response PLR's θ is a weighted average slope). Also causal.py:192-195; stages/causal.py:232-245.

statement: In the partially linear model the omitted-variable bias bound of Chernozhukov et al. 2022 is the final least-squares step's (outcome residual on exposure residual, no intercept), so the Cinelli–Hazlett robustness value of that regression (its classical t on n − 1 df), the median over sample splits, is the lane's required robustness value for DML-PLR on a numeric or yes/no outcome.
regime: inference; DML-PLR
user_sees: Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding is reported by the Cinelli–Hazlett robustness value of the final least-squares step, the outcome's residual on the exposure's (the form the omitted-variable boun…
claimed_basis: Chernozhukov, Cinelli, Newey, Sharma & Syrgkanis 2022, NBER w30302; Cinelli & Hazlett 2020; MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 10
notes: test_1c tests that the code computes F (sensemakr's RV of R's lm(u ~ 0 + v), median over splits), not that F bounds DML's bias. Also models/causal.py:637-640, 665-668; causal.py:542-547.

statement: For a yes/no outcome, the interactive model's marginal risk ratio is the ratio μ₁/μ₀ of its doubly robust means from the same cross-fitted nuisances (for the ATT, the exposed's observed risk over their doubly robust risk unexposed), with the log ratio's variance by the delta method from the same scores, aggregated on the log scale; its E-value is the lane's required sensitivity analysis there.
regime: inference; yes/no exposure and outcome; DML-IRM
decision: the reported risk ratio and its E-value
user_sees: Marginal risk ratio / Risk ratio among the exposed (rows beside the risk difference)
claimed_basis: the delta method; survey's svycontrast as the test's reference
notes: Implementation check (R glm and svycontrast on the same folds, DoubleML's means) plus one data set whose true RR is within 3 SE. Also models/causal.py:47-52, 728-744; causal.py:602-604.

statement: For a yes/no outcome, when one exposure level has no events its risk is zero, so a ratio of the two risks is 0 or undefined and an E-value of it is meaningless, and when one level has only events its odds are infinite and no odds ratio is defined; such ratios and their E-values are not reported, while the risk difference stands.
regime: inference; yes/no outcome; a level with no events or only events
decision: which ratios and E-values are reported
user_sees: no exposed row has the event, so the exposed risk is zero and a ratio of the two risks is 0 or undefined
claimed_basis: by definition
notes: Definitional; test_2c checks the refusal and message (behavior). Also models/causal.py:764-766 (a non-positive doubly robust risk in a split); stages/causal.py:779-783; causal.py:804-810. A level with one event is not flagged.

statement: A random forest's propensities and outcome predictions are too noisy on fewer than 500 rows, so the default nuisance learner is the cross-validated lasso below 500 complete rows and a random forest (200 trees, at least 5 rows per leaf) from 500 rows.
regime: inference; DML or TMLE with no learner named
user_sees: its nuisance models fit by random forests (200 trees, at least 5 rows per leaf)
claimed_basis: none stated beyond the docstring
notes: No simulation compares the defaults; the forest's settings carry no stated reason (models/causal.py:453-458). Also stages/causal.py:37; causal.py:1129-1140.

statement: Fewer than 20 complete rows (or fewer than 20 rows, or one exposure level, left after trimming) are too few to cross-fit any nuisance model, so the lane withholds its estimate.
regime: inference; causal lane
user_sees: Only 15 complete rows: too few to cross-fit anything.
claimed_basis: none stated
notes: An app convention (20 rows over 5 folds trains on 16). Also stages/causal.py:722-725.

statement: Below the unit floor the lane's cluster-robust variance rests on too few units to give an interval, and switching the primary model to a random-intercept mixed model does not repair the lane, so it is withheld with 'keep the primary model only' or 'combine each unit's rows' as the ways forward.
regime: inference; clusters fewer than min_clusters
decision: the lane's withheld estimate and exits
user_sees: `site` has 5 units, fewer than the 12 TurboTab requires for cluster-robust intervals ... Keep the primary model only
claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE §2 ('refusal below a floor'); floor from models.inference.min_clusters (other slice)
notes: test_9 checks the exits (behavior).

statement: For an outcome followed over time with censoring (and possibly staggered entry), a time-to-event analysis such as Cox regression should be used, so Cox proportional hazards is the family the app fits for a time-to-event outcome.
regime: time-to-event task (event plus follow-up time, optional entry)
decision: which family a time-to-event outcome gets
user_sees: Hazard ratios for a time-to-event outcome, using every row's follow-up, censored or not.
claimed_basis: PROBAST (Moons et al. 2019, item 4.6), quoted at survival.py:9-11; AUDIT_REPORT §5 WP12 (RO-03)
notes: Cox is the only family declaring time_to_event; the PROBAST item is about prognostic models, and the app also uses Cox for inference. test_3_a_time_to_event_outcome_gets_only_a_family_that_declares_it checks routing.

statement: Maximizing Cox's partial likelihood with Efron's approximation for tied event times, each row at risk only when entry < t ≤ time (left truncation), gives the hazard-ratio estimates and model-based Wald standard errors that R's coxph and lifelines report, including under heavy ties and delayed entry.
regime: time-to-event; independent rows
decision: the Cox estimate and its intervals
user_sees: 95% Wald intervals from the Cox partial likelihood's information (Efron ties).
claimed_basis: Efron 1977; the default of R's coxph and lifelines
notes: Independent references (lifelines with entry_col, statsmodels PHReg) for 'F is the estimator'. Also survival.py:13-19, 247-297, 514-516.

statement: When rows repeat within a unit, the Lin–Wei cluster-robust sandwich by unit (from Efron-consistent score residuals, no small-sample adjustment) on a t(G − 1) reference, refused below the unit floor, gives valid intervals for the Cox log hazard ratios; t(G − 1) is the least small-sample allowance Cameron & Miller (2015) ask of any cluster-robust interval.
regime: time-to-event; inference; rows repeating within units
user_sees: 95% intervals from the Lin–Wei cluster-robust sandwich by `unit`, G = 40 clusters, on t(39).
claimed_basis: Lin & Wei 1989; Cameron & Miller 2015; R coxph(cluster = …)
notes: Implementation check (the infinitesimal jackknife from lifelines refits); no coverage test. MODELING_SEQUENCE §2 asks CR2 with Bell–McCaffrey df for repeated units; Cox uses CR0 (survival.py:511), and below FEW_CLUSTERS only a concern is added (507-510). Also survival.py:20-23.

statement: Grambsch & Therneau's approximate test on scaled Schoenfeld residuals against event rank, at p below 0.01 shared over the P columns (0.01/P), flags that a covariate's hazard ratio may change over follow-up, and then the reported hazard ratio is an average over follow-up, not one constant ratio.
regime: time-to-event; Cox fit converged
decision: the proportional-hazards concern on the table
user_sees: The hazard ratio for `x` may change over follow-up (Grambsch–Therneau p = 0.0003, against 0.01 shared over 2 columns): it is then an average over follow-up, not one constant ratio.
claimed_basis: Grambsch & Therneau 1994; lifelines proportional_hazard_test(time_transform='rank'); MODELING_SEQUENCE §1 row 11
notes: Partial: p-values equal lifelines' (implementation); on one seeded crossing-hazards fixture it warns and on one PH fixture it is silent. R's cox.zph defaults to the KM transform. 'An average over follow-up' holds only approximately (a weighting that depends on censoring). PH_ALPHA and the Bonferroni sharing are conventions (survival.py:60). Inconsistent thresholds: the effects stage declares an exposure PH failure at p < 0.05 on its own term (stages/effects.py:1226, S6-024).

statement: Under a survey-weighted Cox model, an unweighted Grambsch–Therneau test among the analyzed participants is an adequate check of the model's proportional-hazards form (not a design-based test), and if the hazard ratio changes in the population too the weighted hazard ratio is an average over follow-up.
regime: time-to-event; survey design; population estimand
decision: the proportional-hazards concern on the survey table
user_sees: Among these participants, unweighted, the hazard ratio for `x` may change over follow-up (...): a check of the model's form, not a design-based test.
claimed_basis: none stated
notes: Under informative sampling the sample's and the population's hazard shapes can differ. Merged duplicate: models/survey.py:1234 labels the Schoenfeld (and Brant proportional-odds) checks under the population answer as diagnostics on these participants, not design-based tests. Inconsistent across stages: the effects stage withholds the proportional-hazards test (and Cook's distance) for a design-based model (stages/effects.py:1181, S6-022), while the fit stage reports the unweighted test as an adequate check.

statement: Under the surveyed-population answer, Binder's pseudo-likelihood Cox fit (each row weighted in every risk set, tied Efron slots at their mean weight) with the design-based variance of the total of weighted score residuals, sandwiched by the inverse weighted information over the full design with out-of-domain rows at score zero, is the design-consistent population hazard-ratio estimator and its variance (R survey::svycoxph).
regime: time-to-event; survey design; population estimand
user_sees: survey-weighted Cox proportional hazards (Binder's pseudo-likelihood, Efron ties)
claimed_basis: Binder 1992; survey::svycoxph; MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 6 (MS4)
notes: Independent R reference for 'F is svycoxph' (coefficients 1e-6, SEs 1e-4 relative per its docstring). Also survival.py:158-192 (weighted risk sets). Merged duplicate: the survey contract states the same estimator (models/survey.py:1226).

statement: When the Newton fit drives a coefficient beyond 20 SDs of its column on the log-hazard scale (or does not converge), the partial likelihood has no finite maximum (monotone likelihood, 'in one of its groups every row has the event, or none does'), so the hazard ratio is infinite and no interval or p-value is reported.
regime: time-to-event
user_sees: The partial likelihood has no maximum for `x` (in one of its groups every row has the event, or none does), so the hazard ratio is infinite and no interval or p-value is reported.
claimed_basis: none stated (survival.py:59: 'a log hazard ratio of 20 per SD is an infinite one')
notes: Monotone likelihood in Cox arises when a covariate orders the risk sets perfectly (e.g. a group with no events); a group where every row has the event does not by itself make it monotone, and non-convergence for other reasons gets the same message. Also survival.py:573-581.

statement: For a Cox model fewer than 10 events per predictor (Peduzzi et al. 1995) makes the fit 'fair' and fewer than 5 'poor', and no more events than predictors means the partial likelihood cannot separate them; the family's assessment and concerns say so.
regime: time-to-event
decision: the family assessment (fit label and concerns)

statement: When a time-varying covariate is both a confounder of later exposure and affected by earlier exposure, standard regression (pooled, mixed or GEE) is biased for the effect of the exposure history either way (adjusting for it removes the part of the earlier exposure's effect through it; leaving it out leaves later exposure confounded), so standard regression is refused unless that bias is recorded, the g-methods are the exits, and the standard fit's exposure row is labeled not the effect.
regime: inference; long data; time-varying yes/no exposure; at least one confounder affected by prior exposure (by the answers)
user_sees: Standard regression is biased either way: adjusting for it removes the part of an earlier effect that runs through it, and leaving it out leaves later values of what you study confounded
claimed_basis: Robins, Hernán & Brumback 2000, Epidemiology 11:550 (abstract quoted)
notes: Known-truth simulation (null effect, 20,000 people, one DGP with an unmeasured cause of the confounder and the event): standard pooled logistic regressions are far from 0 adjusted or not; the MSM is within 3 SE. Also time_varying.py:30-42, 183-194, 426-452 (fit_note); stages/time_varying.py:1106-1112.

statement: In long data, a covariate the adjustment answers call a cause or possible cause of the exposure that the exposure could have changed (after_exposure = yes), and a cause of the outcome or a proxy for an unmeasured one, and not an instrument, is a time-varying confounder affected by prior exposure, which every g-method must adjust for at each time point.
regime: inference; long data; time-varying exposure
decision: which covariates trigger the leash and must be time-varying confounders

notes: The answers were designed for a point exposure; here 'could the exposure have changed it' is read as 'affected by prior exposure'. Also time_varying.py:790-800.

statement: With no time-varying confounder affected by prior exposure, standard regression adjusting for each time-varying covariate at each time point blocks no part of the exposure's effect and is sound for the time-varying exposure's effect, so it is the recommended option, with the g-methods still available.
regime: inference; long data; time-varying exposure; no affected confounder

statement: When a confounder affected by prior exposure is present, the marginal structural model with stabilized inverse-probability weights is the recommended g-method (customary in epidemiology; needs a correct model of the exposure and positivity), ranked above the parametric g-formula (less common; needs correct models for every time-varying covariate and the outcome).

claimed_basis: Robins, Hernán & Brumback 2000; Cole & Hernán 2008; Robins 1986; McGrath et al. 2020
notes: The MSM also needs a correctly specified MSM (outcome model), which its 'sound' text omits. Also time_varying.py:148-158.

statement: An exposure measured at the same time as (or not known to precede) the outcome it is paired with cannot be told from a consequence of that outcome (reverse causation), so the g-methods, which need each time point's exposure and covariates to precede the paired outcome, are refused, and standard regression is allowed only as a recorded description with its exposure row labeled open to reverse causation.
regime: inference; long data; ordering answered same time or unknown
user_sees: `x` is measured at the same time as the outcome it is paired with, so its estimate cannot be told from a consequence of the outcome. g-methods need each time point's value ... to precede the outcome
claimed_basis: Hernán & Robins, What If ch. 19 (docstring)
notes: test_4_standard_regression_of_a_concurrent_exposure_is_block_and_record checks behavior. Also time_varying.py:22-28, 195-204, 426-447.

statement: An exposure that takes one value within every unit does not change over time, so the time-varying question does not apply and the standard model estimates its effect.
regime: inference; long data; exposure constant within every unit
user_sees: `x` takes one value within every unit, so it does not change over time; the standard model estimates it.
claimed_basis: none stated
notes: The standard model's validity then rests on the point-exposure adjustment answers.

statement: Stabilized inverse-probability-of-treatment weights (cumulative products within unit of pooled-logistic probabilities of the observed exposure; numerator given the baseline covariates, the previous exposure for an exposure that switches, and time; denominator adding the time-varying confounders; fit on every row, or on rows up to first exposure for initiation) make a pseudo-population in which a weighted MSM of current or cumulative exposure, the baseline covariates and time estimates the effect of the exposure history.

With summary = current the numerator conditions on past exposure that the MSM omits (as Hernán et al. 2000 did); the referee may check that pairing. Also stages/time_varying.py:677-723, 785-790.

statement: With a loss-to-follow-up indicator (1 on a unit's last observed time point before loss), a row's censoring weight is the inverse probability of having stayed through the previous time point (ipwtm's 'cens' product read at the unit's previous row; models fit on rows at risk of loss, so not on event rows), because that row's outcome was seen; the product at the row itself would add a factor depending on that time's confounders and unbalance them.

notes: The test checks the code computes R's product lagged by one row (implementation), not that the lag is the right weight. Censoring models also condition on current exposure (stages/time_varying.py:687-688).

statement: Truncating stabilized weights at progressively narrower percentiles trades bias for precision (each step adds bias and removes variance), while untruncated weights are unbiased if the weight models are right, with extreme weights widening the interval.

statement: Truncation at the 1st and 99th percentiles is customary (Cole & Hernán 2008), and at the 5th and 95th percentiles Cole & Hernán found the precision gained outweighed by the bias.

user_sees: more bias for more precision; Cole & Hernán found the precision gained outweighed by the bias

statement: For the weighted MSM, the unit-clustered CR2 sandwich on the weighted model's working linear model with Bell–McCaffrey degrees of freedom gives a small-sample interval that, because it treats the estimated weights as known, is conservative.

Also time_varying.py:231-235; stages/time_varying.py:1115-1123.

statement: 10,000 simulated units bound the g-formula's Monte Carlo error near 0.005 for a risk of 0.3, so 10,000 is the default simulation size when the analyst declares only the bootstrap count (and the size the cost probe times).

statement: A pooled logistic model of an event at each time point is a discrete-time hazard model, so the MSM's odds ratio is read as a hazard ratio for its E-value, with rarity judged by the cumulative risk by the end of follow-up (below 15%: HR ≈ RR; else (1 − 0.5^√HR)/(1 − 0.5^√(1/HR))); for a repeated yes/no outcome the OR is read as a risk ratio when the outcome is in under 15% of rows, else as √OR.
regime: inference; MSM lane; yes/no outcome
user_sees: the pooled logistic odds ratio as a hazard ratio of an outcome common by the end of follow-up (31.2% cumulative risk), as (1 − 0.5^√HR)/(1 − 0.5^√(1/HR))
claimed_basis: VanderWeele & Ding 2017; R EValue evalues.HR(rare = …)
notes: test_e_values_match_EValue and test_e_value_reads_the_pooled_logistic_ratio_as_a_hazard_ratio_by_cumulative_risk check the formulas (implementation). The OR approximates the discrete-time HR only when each interval's hazard is small; it is read as an HR regardless. Also models/time_varying.py:779-821.

statement: The g-methods here have no design-based estimator, so under the surveyed-population answer their estimates would describe the sample, not the surveyed population, and their intervals would ignore strata and PSUs; the estimates are blocked with the sample-only attestation as the exit, while the outcome-free diagnostics are still shown.

claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 6 and §4 (MS4)
notes: test_4_under_the_surveyed_population_the_estimates_are_blocked_with_the_sample_only_exit checks behavior.

statement: The truncation (or the g-formula's size) must be declared only after this lane's own outcome-free diagnostics (weight distribution, each truncation option's effect, positivity at each time point, the simulation's time) have been shown on the current data, so no analysis choice is informed by an estimate; a change to the data or to an answer the weights read re-asks it.

statement: A covariate that changes within units is time-varying and must enter the g-methods as a time-varying confounder (denominator only), not as a baseline covariate (which enters the stabilized weights' numerator and the MSM).

statement: The weights and the g-formula read each unit's values in time order, so a missing value at any time point, a unit starting after the first time point, a skipped time point, or two rows at one time point breaks the unit's history, and the lane refuses to estimate (multiple imputation of long data for g-methods is not offered).
regime: inference; MSM or g-formula lane

claimed_basis: none stated

statement: With two or more error-prone intakes (or scale scores) in one outcome model, calibrating each on its own while the others are treated as exact leaves bias that can go toward or away from the null, whereas calibrating all of them jointly (multivariate regression calibration, Rosner, Spiegelman & Willett 1990) removes it under classical, mutually independent errors; so one-at-a-time calibration is refused and joint calibration is implied.
regime: inference; linear, logistic or proportional-odds outcome model with >=2 error-prone exposures (recall-measured intakes, e.g. energy beside an adjusted nutrient, every all-components source; or >=2 corrected scale scores)
user_sees: Option 'Each intake calibrated on its own while the others stay uncorrected' labeled "Unsound with several error-prone intakes: the attenuation factor is wrong and the bias can go either way ... neve…
claimed_basis: Rosner, Spiegelman & Willett 1990 (Am J Epidemiol 132:734); Freedman et al. 2011 (JNCI 103:1086) 'may become attenuated, inflated, or can even change direction'; MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 7, §2
notes: Also calibration.py:1-14 (docstring), :854 (relation 'multivariate'), methods/scales.py:72-88 and :571 (calibrate_jointly), core/scales.py:197 (relation). Scales-side known-truth test: turbotab/core/tests/acceptance/test_scales_repair.py::test_4_by_simulation_joint_calibration_recovers_both_coefficients_where_separate_ones_do_not. Joint calibration assumes errors independent across scores (scales) but estimates the full within-person error covariance for recalls (calibration.py), so the regimes differ slightly. Doc: MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 7 ('Multivariate calibration (Rosner 1990) is in v2').

statement: The regression-calibration equation must condition on every other covariate of the outcome model (and never on the outcome), because the attenuation factor that biases the outcome-model slope is the reliability conditional on those covariates; a calibration on the error-prone exposure alone gives the wrong correction.
regime: inference; regression calibration of recall-measured intakes or scale scores with covariates Z in the outcome model
decision: which variables enter the calibration model
user_sees: Relation: "The calibration equation holds every other column of the outcome model, and never the outcome (Boe et al. 2023)." Methods text: "regression calibration including all model covariates"

notes: Also calibration.py:18-22, core/scales.py:179 and methods/scales.py:49-71. The cited test is a known-truth simulation for the scales version (conditional vs marginal attenuation). turbotab/core/tests/acceptance/test_ms5_regression_calibration.py::test_1_every_outcome_model_covariate_is_in_the_calibration_and_never_the_outcome only checks the code includes them (not a test of the claim). Plan doc: MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 7, §2 'implies every outcome-model covariate in the calibration model'.

statement: Within the whole-chain bootstrap under multiple imputation ('Boot MI'), imputing each bootstrap replicate 5 times gives percentile intervals with valid coverage, with the point estimate taken as the mean over the analysis's own m imputations.

statement: Under a complex survey design, resampling PSUs within strata by Rao & Wu's rescaling bootstrap (n_h - 1 PSUs drawn with replacement, weights multiplied by n_h/(n_h - 1)), and resampling a stratum with a single PSU 'twice or not at all, each with chance 1/2', gives the calibrated coefficient a design-consistent variance that matches R survey's lonely.psu = "adjust" treatment used by the primary analysis.

With no stratum of two PSUs the calibration is blocked (calibration.py:892-897). Merged duplicate: models/survey.py:1181 states the same rule in the survey contract (S4 slice). Related: the primary design-based table centers a lonely PSU by R survey's 'adjust' rule (models/survey.py:216, S4 entry); the NCI usual-intake stage instead refuses lonely PSUs (core/usual_intake.py:544).

statement: The regression-calibration estimator implemented (Carroll et al. 2006 §4.4 best linear approximation of E[X | W̄, Z] from replicate data, with pooled within-person covariance) equals R mecor's MeasErrorRandom calibration when every person has the same number of recalls, and for a least-squares outcome model the refit coefficient equals the uncorrected coefficient vector premultiplied by (Γᵀ)⁻¹ (with one intake, divided by the attenuation factor λ, Rosner, Willett & Spiegelman 1989).

statement: With one error-prone exposure and nondifferential classical error, the uncorrected model's test of no association remains valid (only the estimate is attenuated), so the uncorrected estimate is sound as the primary analysis and the reported test for a calibrated analysis stays the uncorrected model's.

statement: With covariates in the model, the slope of an error-prone score is attenuated by its reliability conditional on the covariates, so dividing the coefficient by the marginal α or ω (the Spearman correction) under-corrects whenever the score correlates with the covariates; regression calibration conditional on the covariates is used instead.

notes: Also methods/scales.py:49-71. Known-truth simulation test present.

statement: The error variance of a scale score for regression calibration is (1 - ω)·var(W) from internal consistency, using ω-hierarchical for a multidimensional scale so that group-factor variance counts as error about the general construct; the attenuation factor is λ = (s²_W|Z - σ²_U)/s²_W|Z and for least squares the corrected coefficient equals the uncorrected one divided by λ.

notes: The mecor test verifies the arithmetic given σ²_U, not that (1 - ω_h)var(W) is the right error variance; concern text at stages/scales.py:638-642. Treating (1-ω)var(W) as classical error variance assumes ω is a reliability of the sum in its own units (methods/scales.py:42-47 rescales by item SDs).

statement: Change-in-estimate selection among covariates already judged pre-exposure causes cannot detect mediators or colliders, and for an odds ratio or hazard ratio with a common outcome the estimate changes from non-collapsibility even without confounding, so it is block-and-record under inference and conflicts with OR/HR estimands for common outcomes.
regime: inference; data-driven adjustment by change-in-estimate; OR or HR with a common outcome for the invalidity part
user_sees: Block-and-record label stating it cannot see mediators or colliders and is invalid for an OR or HR with a common outcome
claimed_basis: MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 1(c); §2 'an OR or HR with a common outcome conflicts with change-in-estimate'
notes: Doc-level; check estimand.py (slice S6) for an implementation. No implementation found: grep for change-in-estimate over turbotab/ (non-test code) returns nothing, so this ruling is doc-only at present.
